stories.brief: Fictional mini-stories practicing today's batch from the fifty common Hebrew verbs.
A collection of independent short practical situations from ordinary daily life.

shortItems.brief: A customer withdraws cash at a bank for a small family gathering, asks for some smaller notes, receives a mix of note sizes, and counts the cash before leaving.

storyPattern.goal: Get cash in denominations suited to an immediate household need
storyPattern.interaction: State a preference for smaller notes and check the cash received
storyPattern.outcome: Leave with the requested mix of notes

shortItems.brief: Two roommates compare their notes, see that Yael has already paid part of a household bill, agree that 200 shekels remain, and have one roommate pay that amount while the other records it.

storyPattern.goal: Avoid paying a shared bill twice after a partial payment
storyPattern.interaction: Compare payment notes and agree on what remains
storyPattern.outcome: Pay the remaining amount and record it

shortItems.brief: A resident organizing benefit papers finds a receipt for the electricity bill, labels it clearly, and puts it with her papers while remaining unsure whether anything else is needed.

storyPattern.goal: Make one household expense easy to identify in benefit paperwork
storyPattern.interaction: Find the relevant receipt and label what it records
storyPattern.outcome: Keep the labeled receipt with the paperwork while leaving other requirements open

shortItems.brief: A woman needs to transfer money for a household purchase. She notices that the amount in the app differs from the amount on her note, checks the receipt, corrects her note, and sends the correct amount.

storyPattern.goal: Send the correct amount for a shared household purchase
storyPattern.interaction: Compare the amount in the app with a receipt and correct a personal note
storyPattern.outcome: Send the amount that matches the receipt

shortItems.brief: A resident writing benefit paperwork describes a recent household change: her sister moved in last month. She asks a service worker whether the sentence is clear. The worker confirms that it is understandable without stating what documents are required.

storyPattern.goal: Describe a household change plainly in benefit paperwork
storyPattern.interaction: Offer a brief factual description and ask whether it is clear
storyPattern.outcome: Keep the understandable wording without assuming further requirements

shortItems.brief: A woman sees a small recurring charge in her bank account, checks the transaction details to find its date, and writes the date beside her household expenses.

storyPattern.goal: Record when a known recurring payment was made
storyPattern.interaction: Open a transaction detail and identify its date
storyPattern.outcome: Add the date to a household expense note

shortItems.brief: A woman comes to collect a parcel. She enlarges the message on her phone, reads the unclear code aloud, and the clerk finds and hands her the parcel.

storyPattern.goal: Read a parcel collection code accurately
storyPattern.interaction: Enlarge a message on the recipient's own phone and repeat the code
storyPattern.outcome: The clerk locates and hands over the matching parcel

shortItems.brief: At a supermarket self-checkout, a shopper notices she selected tomatoes even though she put cucumbers in her bag. She cancels the selection, chooses cucumbers, and checks that the screen shows them.

storyPattern.goal: Make the self-checkout record match the produce in the bag
storyPattern.interaction: Cancel an incorrect selection and choose the right item
storyPattern.outcome: Confirm the screen shows the selected produce

shortItems.brief: Dana reviews two data options on her household phone account, asks a representative to explain the difference, and chooses the option that fits how her household uses its phones.

storyPattern.goal: Choose a phone plan option that matches household use
storyPattern.interaction: Ask for a plain-language comparison and state a preference
storyPattern.outcome: Select the option that fits the household's stated needs

shortItems.brief: At a market, a shopper asks for a small amount of mushrooms. The seller weighs a portion, and the shopper accepts it as enough and takes it.

storyPattern.goal: Buy only the amount of a weighed food that is needed
storyPattern.interaction: Ask for a small portion and respond to the weighed amount
storyPattern.outcome: Accept a suitable portion and take it

shortItems.brief: An account holder notices that a recurring household payment is linked to an old card. She checks the two card labels in her account settings, selects the current card for future payments, and sees the updated choice on screen.

storyPattern.goal: Direct future recurring payments to the intended card
storyPattern.relationship: Account holder managing a household payment
storyPattern.interaction: Compare card labels in account settings and select the current card
storyPattern.outcome: See the selected card listed for future payments

translations.en: with the rest of the papers

stories.brief: Tamar visits the bank to separate her future personal card purchases from her partner's joint household account. A clerk shows her the available accounts and explains that the change affects future purchases only. Tamar selects her personal account and later checks that a small card purchase appears there, while the joint account remains available for household expenses.

storyPattern.goal: Direct future card purchases to the intended account
storyPattern.interaction: Explain a spending preference, review account choices, and clarify what the change affects
storyPattern.outcome: Select the personal account and verify a later purchase appears there

stories.brief: At a neighborhood market, Rafi buys an amount of olives suitable for dinner for four. He clarifies that he wants the olives weighed with little brine, checks the portion, and takes the agreed amount home.

storyPattern.goal: Buy a suitable quantity of a weighed food item
storyPattern.interaction: Clarify how the olives are weighed, check the portion, and adjust it
storyPattern.outcome: Take home the agreed quantity for dinner

stories.brief: Liat updates the delivery instructions because repair work has blocked her building's usual entrance. She gives the delivery agent the side gate and bell details, corrects the apartment number, checks the updated details, and tells the doorman where to expect the parcel.

storyPattern.goal: Make delivery access instructions match a temporary change at home
storyPattern.interaction: Explain the access change, give an alternative location, and correct a detail in the agent's repeat-back
storyPattern.outcome: Confirm accurate instructions and alert the doorman

stories.brief: Roommates Noa and Gil notice a recurring charge for their household streaming subscription. Noa thought the subscription was paused, while Gil recalls using it recently and wants to keep it if they can identify the charge. Noa compares the billing description with her account screen, clarifies that it is the household plan rather than an individual add-on, and updates the shared expense note. They agree to keep the service for now.

storyPattern.goal: Identify a recurring digital-service charge and decide how to handle it
storyPattern.relationship: Roommates sharing expenses, with one owning the account
storyPattern.interaction: Compare a billing description with the account holder's screen, clarify a mistaken assumption, and state different preferences
storyPattern.outcome: Keep the service for now and record the charge clearly in the shared expense note

stories.brief: Dana asks her brother Amir to identify his current bank-account entry from a message on his own phone. She confirms the recipient details and repayment amount, sends the transfer herself, and Amir confirms he received it.

storyPattern.goal: Send a repayment to the correct recipient account
storyPattern.relationship: Siblings settling a shared household purchase
storyPattern.interaction: Dana checks the nickname and final digits from Amir's message, confirms the amount against their receipt, and reviews the details before sending
storyPattern.outcome: Dana sends the transfer herself, and Amir confirms that he received it

stories.brief: Yiddish theater became a popular gathering place for Jewish immigrants in the United States, with plays reflecting their language, experiences, and concerns.

sources.title: The Yiddish Theater in America: A Brief Historical Overview

storyBeats: Yiddish theater began in 1876 in Iași, Romania, and reached New York six years later.
Abraham Goldfaden built dramatic performances from popular songs and lyrics, working with singer Israel Gradner and adding dialogue and stage action.
Goldfaden wrote, composed, directed, and designed sets for some of his productions; his plays included The Witch and The Two Kuni Lemls.
After Russia prohibited Yiddish theater in 1883, performers and playwrights joined the migration west; New York became a major center for the form.
Yiddish-speaking Jewish immigrants in New York could see plays in a language they understood, and the stage presented stories about their history and concerns.
The theater drew people across social lines, including rich and poor, educated and illiterate, and religiously observant and free-thinking audiences.
Performances ranged from sentimental dramas and operettas to experiments influenced by European theater.
In 1927, the United States had 24 Yiddish theaters; 11 were in New York, four in Chicago, and three in Philadelphia.
For the 1937–1938 season, an estimate put New York City sales at 1.75 million tickets to Yiddish shows.
Immigration restrictions after 1924, the Great Depression, and competition from radio and movies contributed to the theater’s decline.

stories.brief: Jenő Dick’s memories of Jewish family life in Budapest include holiday food, a kosher pastry shop where his sister worked, and the pastries she shared with him on the way to school.
storyBeats: Jenő Dick recalled growing up in a large Jewish family in Hungary, first in Sátoraljaújhely and later in Miskolc.
One of his sisters lived and worked at a kosher pastry shop because there were many children in the family.
A pastry chef from a Budapest shop taught his sister to make specialized cakes.
On his way to grammar school, Dick stopped at the shop, where his sister gave him cream-pastry end pieces for his snack.
Dick said he sometimes shared the pastry with school friends; at home, even getting an egg could be a luxury.
His family ate foods including cornmeal, bean soup, meat soup, and goose; his mother prepared meat according to kosher practice.
On Saturdays, Dick and his father brought home the cholent his mother had prepared the day before and left warming at a baker’s oven.
For Passover, the family used a separate set of dishes from its everyday dishes.
The family’s girls earned money sewing and hemming aprons; after saving, they bought a Singer sewing machine.
The family moved to Miskolc in 1930 because of poverty, and Dick recalled that they could not afford the rent on their first apartment there.
